newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Canada has made no decision on Pol Pot.
newsitem.headline: Canada has made no decision on Pol Pot.

text.p: Canada has made no decision on a U.S. request to allow captured Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot to be extradited there for trial but "if we can do something we will," Prime Minister Jean Chretien said on Tuesday.

Speaking at the United Nations, where he is attending an environmental Earth Summit, Chretien said Canada had been put on the spot by the request to take Pol Pot so he can be tried by an international tribunal.
Chretien said the whole debate so far was hypothetical because, "We don't know exactly where he is ... and we don't know what we can do legally, if our legislation could apply in the circumstances.
"We have to analyse it in terms of can we do something. Of course, if we can do something we will."
In Ottawa, a foreign affairs spokeswoman said Canada wanted the U.N. Security Council to sanction any move to extradite Pol Pot from Cambodia.
"Our current position is any process to bring Pol Pot to justice should be based on the authorisation of the international community through the U.N. Security Council," Jennifer Ledwidge said.
"I think we're looking more at what the international effort might be ... and how Canada might be able to fit into an international effort," she added.

The Security Council posed its own problems. China, which has a veto on the council, hinted on Tuesday that it was opposed to setting up an international tribunal for Pol Pot, who it has supported at times in the past.
"It should be decided (by) Cambodians themselves without foreign interference," said Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Cui Tiankai.

A United Nations spokesman said that either the Security Council or the General Assembly could create a tribunal to try Pol Pot. The Council has set up tribunals to try people for war crimes in Rwanda and in the former Yugoslavia.

Both Cambodia's two prime ministers say they want Pol Pot sent out of the country to face international justice for crimes against humanity. They fear his continued presence in Cambodia could lead to violence.
Pol Pot is blamed for the slaughter of more than one million Cambodians after his Khmer Rouge took power in 1975.
Only Canada and Denmark have laws allowing trials for people accused of genocide in other countries, but Canada has no extradition treaty with Cambodia.
U.S. officials say they want Pol Pot extradited to Canada as a temporary measure until a tribunal can be convened to try him under the international Genocide Convention.
They said the aim was not to wait for a tribunal to be created before taking him into custody.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright surprised Canada last weekend when she asked Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy to take a leading role in dealing with Pol Pot.
Ottawa officials are worried any attempt to extradite him may not stand up in Canadian courts.
